5. Discussion

5.1 Astrochronology and the imprint of astronomical cycles through the Ludfordian Biogeochemical Event

The establishment of the astrochronological framework for the Kosov quarry section represents a new step toward quantifying the tempo of the MLCIE, the largest carbon-isotope excursion of the Phanerozoic, LBE, and completing the (Silurian) astronomical timescale. The new anchored astrochronology provides the first virtually complete, high-resolution temporal calibration, allowing us to examine the imprint of astronomical cycles and their role in modulating the processes at play during the LBE. The anchored astrochronological age model was used to assign ages, durations, and associated uncertainties to chrono- and geochronologic units, lithological units, and events in the Kosov section, as tabulated in Table 1. The LBE started at 424.30 ± 0.61 Ma and lasted 1150 ± 260 kyr. In contrast, the LKB (culmination of the Siluricus Ocean Anoxic Event, Frýda et al., (2021b)) lasted only 30 ± 10 kyr. A previous estimate for the onset of the LBE is based on a dated hiatus in the Cellon section, spanning 424.19 ± 0.55 Ma to 423.83 ± 0.55 Ma (Arts et al., 2024). Another age constraint is a U-Pb zircon age of 424.08 ± 0.20 Ma, obtained from a bentonite located less than 1 m below the onset of the positive δ13Ccarb excursion (Cramer et al., 2015). The new astrochronologically tuned age for the onset of the LBE (424.30 ± 0.61) falls within the independently derived age range (when the associated uncertainty is accounted for), thereby reinforcing the robustness of our results. The increase in uncertainty away from the anchor point was reduced by a feature of the anchoring algorithm that checked for the preservation of spectral peaks of known astronomical cycles, thereby rejecting outliers and reducing the increase in uncertainty away from the tie-point. The resulting uncertainty distribution is a continuous semi-objective measure of cyclostratigraphic uncertainty imprint, avoiding the subjectivity of cycle-error counting. The estimated uncertainties in event durations are approximately 15%. Future studies employing a multi-proxy analysis similar to the framework of Arts et al. (2024) may help to further reduce uncertainty and refine the age model for the Kosov quarry. By isolating the precession, obliquity, and the 100 and 405-kyr eccentricity cycles from the tuned induration record, the hierarchical imprint of astronomical forcing becomes particularly clear (Fig. 7G-K). Bed-scale induration alternations are primarily paced by precession and obliquity, whereas their organisation into larger-scale bundles is governed by eccentricity, consistent with its role in modulating precessional amplitude (Hinnov, 2000; Laskar et al, 2004; Laskar, 2020). This systematic bundling reflects the expected structure of astronomically forced climate signals, in which higher-frequency cycles are nested within lower-frequency modulation envelopes. In particular, the modulation of precession by short eccentricity, and of short eccentricity by long eccentricity, defines a coherent hierarchy characteristic of astronomical forcing. The presence of this nested cyclicity further supports the interpretation of a primary climate signal, consistent with the lack of significant diagenetic overprint discussed in Section 3.1. The periods interpreted as obliquity (28 kyr) and precession (16 kyr) cycles are at the shorter end of the typically expected durations for the Silurian (Farhat et al., 2022; Waltham, 2015; Wu et al., 2024), yet remain within the current uncertainty range for the estimated durations of these cycles during the Silurian. Obliquity and precession, but even more so the half precession, are at or even near the resolution of the record, and as such, care should be taken when interpreting these cycles since some of the extracted individual wiggles can be artefacts of the processing of the signal. Complementary EHA and MTM-based spectral analyses do contain clear obliquity and even a clear precession peak at 16 and 20 kyr, while the amplitude of the half-precession is low, so a harmonic origin of the half-precession cycle cannot be discounted (see SI 2). Furthermore, because both the precession and obliquity signals may contain minor harmonic artefacts, parameters derived from their fundamental frequencies, such as estimates of the Earth-Moon distance, would contain an added degree of unquantified uncertainty. Consequently, such calculations were not attempted here and are not considered reliable based on the presented record. A spectral peak of ~55 kyr was observed in the average CWT scalogram (Fig. 7F). This spectral peak could correspond to the 55-kyr or 54-kyr eccentricity cycle or the 52.8-kyr obliquity cycle (Laskar, 2020; Laskar et al., 2004), or could be unrelated to astronomical forcing. The spectral power of the 55-kyr cycle in the CWT scalogram is highly variable, indicating that the 55-kyr cycle might be transient and unrelated to astronomical forcing (Fig. 7F)). A 200-kyr cycle can also be identified in the record (Fig 7F). Given the strong imprint of the 100-kyr and 405-kyr eccentricity cycles, it is reasonable to interpret the 200-kyr cycle as the seldom observed 200-kyr eccentricity cycle (Hilgen et al., 2020). Several longer-term trends/cycles can be observed in the data, including a spectral peak at 800-kyr. The 800-kyr can be linked to the 812-kyr obliquity cycle (Hinnov 2000). However, since the record is rather short (2020 kyr), there is substantial uncertainty about whether the 800-kyr cycle is truly astronomical in origin or merely an artefact of underlying long-term non-astronomical trends. The same is true for the impact of the longer cycles, such as the 1.2 Myr obliquity and 2.4 Myr eccentricity cycle, which have been suggested to play a role in pacing Palaeozoic events (Campton et al., 2018; Sproson, 2020; Sproson et al., 2022). To fully understand the impact of astronomical forcing on the LBE, including the long multi-million-year astronomical cycles, substantially longer records are needed.

5.1.1 Phase relationships and eccentricity driven insolation control on induration

The amplitude modulation of astronomical cycles in the induration record provides a critical insight into the phase relationships between proxy signals and “true” astronomical cycles, as well as their connection to insolation changes (Arts et al., 2024; Hinnov, 2000; Laurin et al., 2017; Zeeden et al., 2015). Since amplitude-modulating cycles affect the signal amplitude in a unidirectional manner, the astronomical cycles extracted from amplitude records are in phase with their true astronomical cycle counterparts, regardless of whether the proxy responds positively or negatively to insolation forcing, allowing one to uncover the phase relationship between proxy-derived astronomical cycles, the true astronomical cycles, and insolation variations (Arts et al., 2024; Hinnov, 2000; Laurin et al., 2017; Zeeden et al., 2015)(SI 1). The 100- and 405-kyr eccentricity cycles extracted from the precession and 100-kyr eccentricity amplitude records, respectively, show an anti-phase relationship with the corresponding eccentricity cycles directly extracted from the induration record (Fig. 7G, J). This relationship indicates that minima in the astronomical eccentricity cycles correspond to maxima in the equivalent components extracted from the induration record. The phase relationship provides a mechanistic explanation of how changes in eccentricity-driven insolation influenced bed hardness. During eccentricity maxima, increased seasonal variability likely enhanced runoff and detrital input, thereby suppressing carbonate production and producing softer, shale- and clay-rich beds with lower induration. Conversely, during eccentricity minima, reduced seasonal variability favoured carbonate production and deposition, generating harder, more competent limestone beds with higher induration values (Martinez, 2018; Mutterlose and Ruffell, 1999). Therefore, the induration record directly reflects how variations in eccentricity modulate the carbonate content and physical competence of the deposited sediment. The established relationship between eccentricity and induration can also be used to interpret the imprint of astronomical cycles on the rate of change (‰/kyr) of the δ13Ccarb record. Since the 100-kyr eccentricity cycle extracted from the rate of change (‰/kyr) record is generally in phase with the 100-kyr eccentricity cycle extracted from the induration record, it can be inferred that the δ13Ccarb rate of change (‰/kyr) is the highest during astronomical eccentricity minima (Fig. 7J).

5.2 Evaluating the drivers and pacing of the carbon-cycle during the Ludfordian Biogeochemical Event

The new astrochronologically anchored age model enables the first robust estimation of δ13Ccarb rate-of-change (‰/kyr) values across the Ludfordian Biogeochemical Event (LBE) (Figs. 8,9). Until now, the tempo of major Palaeozoic carbon isotope excursions has remained poorly constrained. Most studies report δ13Ccarb variations as differences across discrete stratigraphic or temporal intervals spanning tens to hundreds of kiloyears, rather than calculating rates of change directly from continuous isotope records (Maloof et al., 2010; Reershemius and Planavsky, 2021; Ma et al., 2022; De Vleeschouwer et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Huygh et al., 2026). Consequently, although the overall magnitude and duration of excursions are well known, their true rates of change remain unresolved, limiting quantitative comparisons among carbon cycle perturbations. By utilising a LOWESS regression of the δ13Ccarb curve to minimise short-term noise and establish a stable regional reference, the calibrated timescale provides continuous age control and allows the first direct estimation of these rates (Fig. 8F). During the excursion, δ13Ccarb rate-of-change values reached a maximum of +0.09 ‰/kyr. This is approximately four times higher than the ~0.02 ‰/kyr estimate derived from the spline-interpolated curve used in the GTS 2020 timescale (Cramer and Jarvis, 2020; Gradstein et al., 2020), a framework relying on spline-interpolated curves that were not designed to capture rapid biogeochemical events (Fig. 9C, E, F). These results demonstrate that δ13Ccarb rate-of-change values depend on the underlying age model and highlight the critical importance of cyclostratigraphic approaches for resolving the dynamics of Palaeozoic events. Consequently, previously reported rates should be systematically re-evaluated using astrochronologically calibrated timescales to enable robust inter-event comparisons and more accurate quantification of carbon cycle dynamics. These findings further indicate that Silurian carbon isotope excursions are characterised not only by unusually large amplitudes but also by comparatively high rates of change, highlighting the extreme sensitivity of the Silurian carbon cycle (Fig 9C, E, F)

5.2.1 Astronomical pacing of carbon cycle dynamics

Beyond quick and large magnitude changes in the δ13Ccarb rate-of-change record, the record also contains a clear imprint of the 100-kyr eccentricity cycle during the R and S zones of the MLCIE (Figs. 8F-G, 9F-G). The highest δ13Ccarb rates-of-change consistently occur during the R and S zones during short astronomical eccentricity minima. This phase relationship suggests that minima in eccentricity dampen the amplitude of climatic precession, thereby decreasing seasonal contrast and producing more stable climatic conditions. These conditions favour the burial and preservation of organic carbon in quasi-stable reservoirs. Given the limited terrestrial biomass of the Silurian, these reservoirs are proposed to have been regions of deep-ocean anoxia that provided the necessary stability for the burial of organic matter (Laurin et al., 2015, 2017; Sproson, 2020; Sproson et al., 2022). These astronomically paced fluctuations in carbon burial could have contributed to transient atmospheric CO₂ drawdown and cooling, facilitating gla

5.2.2 Drivers of the amplified δ13Ccarb rate-of-change signal

While astronomical forcing provides a compelling explanation for the pacing of carbon burial during the LBE, it cannot alone account for the pronounced amplification of rate-of-change values observed during the R and S isotope zones (Figs. 8F-G, 9F-G). Recent evidence suggests the LBE was initiated by an anomalous influx of trace metals into the ocean, which promoted the expansion of shallow-marine anoxia (Frýda et al., 2021a; De Backer et al., 2026). This period of elevated trace metal concentrations persisted for approximately 350 ± 80 kyr (from 424.6 ± 0.65 Ma to 424.25 ± 0.61 Ma), representing a broad interval of perturbed ocean chemistry. Within this window, the Lau-Kozlowskii Event (LKB) marks the primary culmination of the Siluricus Ocean Anoxic Event, characterised by a sharp peak in metal concentrations lasting roughly 30 ± 10 kyr. Increased organic carbon burial under such conditions would have drawn down atmospheric CO₂ and destabilised the climate system. However, this mechanism fails to account for the prolonged volatility of the carbon cycle, as amplified δ13Ccarb rate-of-change values persist throughout the R and S isotope zones (424.27 ± 0.61 to 423.62 ± 0.56 Ma) long after trace metal concentrations have returned to baseline levels (Frýda et al., 2021a; De Backer et al., 2026). A secondary amplification mechanism is therefore required to sustain the observed carbon cycle response. Two distinct frameworks offer plausible secondary amplification pathways via large-scale reorganisation of ocean circulation, decoupling shallow and deep reservoirs. The first involves climatic state switching between the so-called P and S states of the Silurian ocean-climate system (Jeppsson, 1990; Jeppsson et al., 1995; Bickert et al., 1997; Calner, 2008; Cramer and Saltzman, 2005). During the onset of a Silurian event a transition from a humid P-state, characterised by enhanced runoff and marl-dominated sedimentation, to an arid S-state with reduced runoff and widespread carbonate production occurs. Such a state switch also entails a fundamental shift toward a negative evaporation-precipitation balance in low-latitude shelfal areas, which would result in the creation of dense, saline surface waters that activate low-latitude downwelling centres. This process would reorganise ocean circulation patterns, promoting water-column stratification and the development of widespread deep-ocean anoxia, creating a quasi-stable deep-ocean carbon reservoir that increases the carbon cycle’s sensitivity to external forcing (Sproson, 2020; Sproson et al., 2022). Alternatively, Earth system modelling by Pohl et al. (2014, 2021, 2022) emphasises high-latitude processes and demonstrates that Palaeozoic ocean circulation was highly sensitive to atmospheric pCO₂. In Hirnantian simulations by Pohl et al. (2021), progressive cooling associated with declining pCO₂ suppresses the formation of high-latitude deep water. The resulting sluggish circulation and decoupling between the shallow oxygenated and deep anoxic ocean would have made the deep ocean a quasi-stable deep-ocean carbon reservoir sensu Sproson (2020) and Sproson et al. (2022), providing a plausible mechanism for the development of the main phase of the LBE during the R and S isotope zones. Further cooling in the models of Pohl et al. (2021) eventually shifts deep-water formation to southern high latitudes, increasing ocean ventilation. This scenario closely corresponds to the F-zone of the LBE, during which sea level was low (Manda et al., 2012), δ¹³Ccarb values began to decline, and the rate-of-change of δ¹³Ccarb became negative, reflecting the remineralisation of stored organic carbon and the return of isotopically light carbon to the ocean-atmosphere system (Figs. 8F-G, 9F-G). The absence of strong eccentricity pacing during the F-zone suggests that carbon burial was no longer dominated by eccentricity-paced stagnation. Crucially, as pCO₂ began to rise during the F-zone, the climate system would theoretically have recrossed the threshold, returning to the sluggish circulation regime associated with the R and S zones. However, no such secondary perturbation is observed. This discrepancy likely reflects hysteresis-like behaviour in which nonlinear interactions between sea-ice feedbacks and ocean heat transport produce a distinct equilibrium pathway for climatic recovery (Pohl et al., 2014). By following this alternative return branch of the hysteresis loop, the ocean avoided a return to widespread deep-ocean anoxia and instead stabilised into a more ventilated circulation state. Although the P-to-S state model emphasises low-latitude downwelling and the simulations of Pohl et al. (2021) highlight high-latitude downwelling and pCO₂ sensitivity, both frameworks describe large-scale reorganisations of ocean circulation that can reduce deep-ocean ventilation and enhance organic carbon burial. In both scenarios, the deep ocean acts as a quasi-stable reservoir that is sensitive to astronomical forcing (Sproson, 2020; Sproson et al., 2022). However, while the Pohl et al. (2021) framework accounts for system recovery via a hysteresis loop, the P-to-S state-switch framework currently lacks a detailed mechanism to return to the original climatic state. While identifying which of the two circulation models is most accurate will require expanded multi-proxy datasets, the existing δ13Ccarb record can already give insights into the role of astronomical forcing during Silurian ocean circulation switches. The persistence of positive δ13Ccarb rate-of-change values throughout the R and S isotope zones provides a critical insight. Although the 100-kyr eccentricity signal clearly paces the δ13Ccarb rate-of-change record, the values remain consistently positive during these zones, indicating sustained net carbon burial (Figs. 8F-G, 9F-G). If astronomical cycles had repeatedly triggered transitions between contrasting circulation regimes, periodic remineralisation of stored organic carbon would be expected to release isotopically light carbon back into the ocean-atmosphere system. Such behaviour would produce alternating phases of positive and negative δ13Ccarb rate-of-change values on astronomical timescales. The absence of such reversals suggests that astronomical forcing did not repeatedly drive transitions between circulation states. Instead, the system likely crossed a circulation threshold once near the onset of the LBE, after which astronomical cycles paced variations in carbon burial efficiency within a newly established, stable circulation regime.

5.2.3 Reconciling carbon cycle dynamics and sedimentological and geochemical trends during the LBE

When viewed in the context of chemostratigraphic and sedimentological records, these circulation mode switches successfully explain several characteristic features of the LBE. The phase locking of δ13Ccarb rate-of-change maxima to eccentricity minima implies that reduced seasonality and weaker circulation enhanced stratification, allowing an already established deep-ocean carbon reservoir to expand and accumulate carbon under anoxic conditions. Geochemical observations support this interpretation. Rising U δ238U values in the Kosov quarry section indicate a contraction of globally anoxic seafloor areas during the onset of the LBE (del Rey et al., 2023). Rather than contradicting the carbon-isotope signal, this trend reflects a redistribution of carbon burial from progressively oxygenated shallow shelves to an increasingly anoxic deep ocean. While the total area of seafloor anoxia decreased, burial intensified within the isolated anoxic parts of the deep ocean. Because deoxygenated shallow shelves had previously acted as major uranium sinks, their oxygenation during the LBE reduced global uranium burial efficiency and shifted seawater δ²³⁸U toward more oxic values, even as decoupled deep-ocean basins sequestered carbon more effectively, raising δ13C values. Simultaneously, vertical decoupling resolves a Silurian carbon-cycle paradox: the coexistence of enhanced carbonate deposition co-occurring with a major positive δ13C excursion. Within this framework, the transition from marl- and shale-dominated successions to carbonate-rich facies on low-latitude shelves can be readily explained (Aldridge et al., 1993; Cramer and Saltzman, 2007a, 2007b; Jeppsson, 1990, 1993; Jeppsson et al., 1995). Whether driven by low-latitude downwelling during P-to-S transitions or by enhanced high-latitude ventilation under declining pCO₂, both mechanisms result in more oxygenated surface waters while maintaining a stratified, poorly ventilated deep ocean. Oxygenated, stable surface waters would have allowed carbonate platforms and reefal systems to develop, while stratified deep basins simultaneously promoted the burial of organic carbon, driving the positive δ¹³C excursion. Astronomical forcing further paced this system. Reduced seasonality during eccentricity minima stabilised runoff and nutrient delivery, promoting carbonate production on shallow shelves while enhancing deep-ocean stratification and organic carbon burial. So, while elevated δ13C rate-of-change values co-occur with carbonate deposition, the two are not directly linked, merely reflecting concurrent responses to the same astronomical forcing.

5.2.4 The LBE as a mechanistic template for interpreting Phanerozoic carbon isotope excursions

Shifts between distinct ocean circulation modes, involving decoupling of the shallow and deep ocean, provide a mechanistic explanation not only for the LBE but also possibly for other large Silurian carbon-cycle excursions, without requiring extreme nutrient input or globally pervasive anoxia. Such circulation changes could have been triggered by relatively modest perturbations to baseline climate, pushing the Silurian ocean system past critical thresholds and tipping points, leading to substantial reorganisation of ocean structure and the redistribution of oxygen and carbon within it. From this perspective, the LBE does not represent an isolated oceanographic anomaly but rather the expression of a latent sensitivity within the Palaeozoic climate system that allowed the ocean to shift between distinct circulation modes. The many similarities between the LBE and the Hirnantian Carbon Isotope Excursion (HICE) suggest that the boundary conditions enabling such behaviour may already have been established by the Late Ordovician. In this framework, the HICE may represent an earlier manifestation of circulation instabilities and carbon cycle reorganisations that continued to influence Silurian oceanography, with subsequent Silurian carbon isotope excursions reflecting repeated or evolving expressions of the same underlying system sensitivity rather than entirely independent phenomena. Within the sequence of Silurian carbon isotope excursions, the LBE emerges as a particularly well-resolved example of Earth system threshold behaviour and therefore provides a rare deep-time benchmark for assessing the sensitivity, pacing, and magnitude of carbon cycle instability. When placed within an astronomically calibrated timescale, the δ13Ccarb rate-of-change proxy is revealed to be paced by the 100-kyr eccentricity cycle, indicating that astronomical forcing acted as a pacemaker of carbon-cycle dynamics during the LBE (Fig. 8, 9). This finding highlights the importance of explicitly incorporating astronomical forcing into future Earth system modelling and stratigraphic studies when investigating the drivers of Silurian carbon-cycle perturbations. Furthermore, concepts such as circulation-mode switching, pCO₂ sensitivity, and the development of an astronomically paced quasi-stable carbon reservoir not only provide a coherent framework for interpreting the contrasting proxy signals and lithological trends of the LBE but also represent fundamental Earth-system behaviours that extend beyond the Silurian (Duplessy and Shackleton, 1985; Batenburg et al., 2016; Laurin et al., 2017; De Vleeschouwer, 2020; Westerhold, 2020; Martinez et al., 2023; Vervoort et al., 2024, 2026). The LBE can thus also serve as a mechanistic template for interpreting other Phanerozoic δ13C excursions, typified by proxy signals and lithological patterns, which appear contradictory. In this context, the LBE not only records a Silurian carbon-cycle perturbation but also illustrates how astronomical forcing, when amplified by threshold behaviour in ocean circulation, can generate rapid, high-amplitude oscillations in the rate of change of δ13Ccarb.

Code 
Ciso <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stratigraphy/Kosov-cyclostrat/main/WholeCIso_Neoprotero_Permian.csv")


### add back Silurian d13C and  d13C rates

CisoPZ <- filter(Ciso, Age != "Neoprotero")
a <- 400
dCiso_kyr <- cbind((Ciso$Time * 1000) + a, Ciso$dCiso)
dCiso_kyr <- sortNave(dCiso_kyr, genplot = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
dCiso_kyr <- linterp(dCiso_kyr, genplot = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

time_kyr <- dCiso_kyr[, 1]
d13C <- dCiso_kyr[, 2]

# Calculate the rate of change in ‰/kyr
rate_of_change <- -1 * diff(d13C) / diff(time_kyr)  # ‰/kyr
midpoints <- head(time_kyr, -1) + diff(time_kyr) / 2  # midpoints for plotting
rate_df <- data.frame(Time_kyr = midpoints, d13C_rate = rate_of_change)

# Define plotting data
ages = dCiso_kyr[, 1] / 1000
data = dCiso_kyr[, 2]

# Mean value
mean_ind <- mean(ind_values, na.rm = TRUE)

# Identify above-mean intervals
above <- ind_values > mean_ind
runs  <- rle(above)
ends  <- cumsum(runs$lengths)
starts <- c(1, head(ends + 1, -1))

# Keep only TRUE segments

                       starts[runs$values],
                       ends[runs$values])

convert[, 2] <- c("Eon", "Era", "Period", "Epoch", "Age")
for (c in 1:length(units)) {

  }

6. Conclusions

he new astrochronology from the Kosov Quarry provides the first continuous, anchored astrochronological framework for the Ludfordian Biogeochemical Event (LBE), encompassing the largest positive δ13Ccarb excursion of the Phanerozoic. The anchored cyclostratigraphic framework indicates that the LBE began at 424.30 ± 0.61 Ma and lasted 1150 ± 260 kyr. Using this framework, δ13Ccarb rate-of-change values reached a maximum of +0.09 ‰/kyr at the onset of the LBE, demonstrating that Silurian carbon-cycle perturbations were not only large in magnitude but also unusually rapid. Both the induration (the degree of rock hardness determined by the concentration and cementation of carbonates) and δ13Ccarb rate-of-change records reveal a pervasive imprint of astronomical cycles, ranging from precession to the 405-kyr eccentricity cycle. Phase relationships derived from amplitude modulation indicate that the induration record is anti-phased with astronomical eccentricity cycles, consistent with reduced runoff and enhanced carbonate production during eccentricity minima. Critically, the δ13Ccarb rate-of-change record contains a strong 100-kyr eccentricity signal, with maxima occurring during astronomical eccentricity minima. This provides the first direct evidence of eccentricity-paced carbon cycle dynamics during the Silurian and establishes the δ13Ccarb rate of change as a powerful proxy for resolving the tempo of deep-time carbon cycle perturbations. While astronomical forcing robustly explains the pacing of carbon burial, it does not account for the sustained amplification of δ¹³Ccarb rate-of-change values during the main phase of the LBE. Instead, the data indicate that the carbon cycle crossed a critical threshold early in the event, resulting in a large-scale reorganisation of ocean circulation. Within the P-S state framework, this threshold is associated with the creation of low-latitude downwelling centres. Conversely, in the model of Pohl et al. (2021), the threshold is defined by a specific pCO2 tipping point that triggers suppression of high-latitude deep-water formation. Whether driven by these low-latitude circulation changes or pCO2-sensitive shifts in high-latitude deep-water formation, both mechanisms converge on the same outcome: a vertically decoupled ocean featuring oxygenated shallow shelves and a stratified, anoxic deep ocean. In this state, the deep ocean acted as a quasi-stable carbon reservoir, facilitating carbon accumulation and enhancing the system’s sensitivity to astronomical forcing. This decoupling redistributed oxygen and carbon burial, promoting carbonate production on shallow shelves and organic carbon storage in the deep ocean, thereby reconciling the co-occurrence of carbonate platform expansion and positive δ¹³C peaks during Silurian biogeochemical events. These findings indicate that large Silurian carbon-isotope excursions did not require extreme external forcing but instead reflect an intrinsically sensitive Earth system capable of crossing circulation thresholds. The LBE thus illustrates how astronomical forcing, amplified by internal feedbacks and ocean circulation reorganisation, can pace high-amplitude carbon-cycle variability.

    abline(v = c(90, 95, 99), lty = 3, col = "grey", lwd = 2)
    if (add_MTM_peaks == TRUE & is.na(MTM_res_2[1, 2]) == 
      FALSE) {
      abline(h = 1/MTM_res_2[, 1], col = "red", lty = 3)
    }
    plot(y = 1/MTM_res_1[, 1], x = MTM_res_1[, 4], type = "l", 
      yaxs = "i", yaxt = "n", xlab = "Ar. conf lvl", ylab = "", 
      log = "y", xlim = c(80, 101), xaxs = "i", ylim = ylim_vals)
    abline(v = c(90, 95, 99), lty = 3, col = "grey", lwd = 2)
    if (add_MTM_peaks == TRUE & is.na(MTM_res_2[1, 2]) == 
      FALSE) {
      abline(h = 1/MTM_res_2[, 1], col = "red", lty = 3)
    }
    plot(y = 1/MTM_res_1[, 1], x = MTM_res_1[, 2], type = "l", 
      yaxs = "i", yaxt = "n", xlab = "MTM power", ylab = "", 
      log = "y", ylim = ylim_vals)
    for (i in 5:8) {
      lines(y = 1/MTM_res_1[, 1], x = MTM_res_1[, i], 
        ylim = ylim_vals, lty = 3, col = "grey", lwd = 2)
    }
    if (add_MTM_peaks == TRUE & is.na(MTM_res_2[1, 2]) == 
      FALSE) {
      abline(h = 1/MTM_res_2[, 1], col = "red", lty = 3)
    }
    par(new = FALSE, mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0), mgp = c(2, 1, 
      0))
    image(x = eha_log2$depth, y = eha_log2$log2_period, 
      z = t(mat), col = key.cols, breaks = power_max_mat.levels, 
      useRaster = TRUE, ylab = periodlab, xlab = x_lab, 
      axes = TRUE, yaxt = "n", main = main, xlim = xlim_vals, 
      ylim = log2(ylim_vals))
    box(lwd = lwd.axis)
    period.tick = unique(trunc(eha_log2$log2_period))
    period.tick = na.omit(period.tick)
    period.tick.label = 2^(period.tick)
    axis(2, lwd = lwd.axis, at = period.tick, labels = NA, 
      tck = periodtck, tcl = periodtcl)
    axis(4, lwd = lwd.axis, at = period.tick, labels = NA, 
      tck = periodtck, tcl = periodtcl)
    mtext(period.tick.label, side = 2, at = period.tick, 
      las = 2, line = par()$mgp[2] - 0.5, font = par()$font.axis, 
      cex = par()$cex.axis)
    if (is.null(add_lines) != TRUE) {
      for (i in 2:ncol(add_lines)) lines(add_lines[, 1], 
        log2(add_lines[, i]))
    }
    if (is.null(add_points) != TRUE) {
      for (i in 2:ncol(add_points)) points(add_points[, 
        1], log2(add_points[, i]))
    }
    if (add_MTM_peaks == TRUE & is.na(MTM_res_2[1, 2]) == 
      FALSE) {
      abline(h = log2(1/MTM_res_2[, 1]), col = "black", 
        lty = 3)
    }
    if (is.null(add_abline_h) != TRUE) {
      abline(h = log2(add_abline_h))
    }
    if (is.null(add_abline_v) != TRUE) {
      abline(v = add_abline_v,col=adjustcolor("grey50", alpha.f = 0.6),lwd=10)
    }
  }
  if (add_data == FALSE & add_avg == FALSE & add_MTM == FALSE & 
    plot_horizontal == TRUE) {
    layout.matrix <- matrix(c(2, 1), nrow = 1, ncol = 2, 
      byrow = TRUE)
    graphics::layout(mat = layout.matrix, heights = c(1), 
      widths = c(10, 2.25))
    power_max_mat.levels = quantile(mat, probs = seq(from = 0, 
      to = 1, length.out = n.levels + 1))
    par(mar = c(4, 0, 2, 5))
    image(y = seq(from = 0, to = n.levels), x = 1, z = (matrix(power_max_mat.levels, 
      nrow = 1)), col = key.cols, breaks = power_max_mat.levels, 
      useRaster = TRUE, yaxt = "n", xaxt = "n", xlab = "", 
      ylab = "", )
    axis(4, lwd = lwd.axis, at = key.marks, labels = NA, 
      tck = 0.02, tcl = 1.24)
    mtext(key.labels, side = 4, at = key.marks, line = 0.5, 
      las = 2, font = par()$font.axis, cex = par()$cex.axis)
    mtext(c("Power"), side = 4, at = mean(key.marks), line = 0.5, 
      las = 2, font = par()$font.axis, cex = par()$cex.axis)
    box(lwd = lwd.axis)
    par(new = FALSE, mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.5))
    image(x = eha_log2$depth, y = eha_log2$log2_period, 
      z = t(mat), col = key.cols, breaks = power_max_mat.levels, 
      useRaster = TRUE, ylab = periodlab, xlab = x_lab, 
      axes = TRUE, yaxt = "n", main = main, xlim = xlim_vals, 
      ylim = log2(ylim_vals))
    box(lwd = lwd.axis)
    period.tick = unique(trunc(eha_log2$log2_period))
    period.tick = na.omit(period.tick)
    period.tick.label = 2^(period.tick)
    axis(2, lwd = lwd.axis, at = period.tick, labels = NA, 
      tck = periodtck, tcl = periodtcl)
    axis(4, lwd = lwd.axis, at = period.tick, labels = NA, 
      tck = periodtck, tcl = periodtcl)
    mtext(period.tick.label, side = 2, at = period.tick, 
      las = 2, line = par()$mgp[2] - 0.5, font = par()$font.axis, 
      cex = par()$cex.axis)
    if (is.null(add_lines) != TRUE) {
      for (i in 2:ncol(add_lines)) lines(add_lines[, 1], 
        log2(add_lines[, i]))
    }
    if (is.null(add_points) != TRUE) {
      for (i in 2:ncol(add_points)) points(add_points[, 
        1], log2(add_points[, i]))
    }
    if (add_MTM_peaks == TRUE & is.na(MTM_res_2[1, 2]) == 
      FALSE) {
      abline(h = log2(1/MTM_res_2[, 1]), col = "black", 
        lty = 3)
    }
    if (is.null(add_abline_h) != TRUE) {
      abline(h = log2(add_abline_h))
    }
    if (is.null(add_abline_v) != TRUE) {
      abline(v = add_abline_v,col=adjustcolor("grey50", alpha.f = 0.6),lwd=10)
    }
  }
  if (add_MTM_peaks == TRUE & is.na(MTM_res_2[1, 2]) == FALSE) {
    return(invisible(mtm_res))
  }
}
